title: URL Shortener
prompt: We want our own short-link service. People paste a long link, get back something like sho.rt/aZ3kQ9x, and anyone who opens it lands on the original page. Owners also want to see how many clicks each link got.

clarify.q: Roughly how many links are created per month, and how many times is a typical link opened?
clarify.why: Write rate decides whether one database primary is enough; the read:write ratio decides how much of the design is really about the redirect path and caching.

clarify.q: Do links expire, and can an owner delete a link or change where it points?
clarify.why: If links can change or die, browsers must not cache the redirect forever, which rules out a permanent 301. It also decides whether storage grows without limit.

clarify.q: Can users pick a custom alias like /spring-sale?
clarify.why: Aliases share the same namespace as generated codes, so the uniqueness check has to cover both and handle two people claiming the same alias at once.

clarify.q: How exact and how fresh must click counts be?
clarify.why: Exact, real-time counts put a database write on every redirect. Counts that are a few minutes late and may miss 0.1% let us move counting off the hot path entirely.

clarify.q: Must codes be hard to guess?
clarify.why: Sequential codes let anyone walk the whole keyspace and find private links (shared documents, invite links). That pushes us to random or scrambled codes.

clarify.q: Is the audience global, and is there a latency target for the redirect?
clarify.why: A global audience with a tight target means caching redirects at the edge or running read replicas in several regions, not one data center.

clarify.q: Do creators sign in or use API keys?
clarify.why: Ownership is needed for stats, edits and deletes, and it gives us a key for per-user quotas against spam.

functional: Create a short link for a long URL; optional custom alias (4–30 chars of a–z, 0–9, hyphen) and optional expiry time.
Opening a short link redirects to the destination; unknown codes return 404 and expired or deleted links return 410.
Retrying a create with the same Idempotency-Key returns the original link instead of a second one.
The owner can delete a link or change its expiry.
The owner can see total and per-day click counts for each link.
nonFunctional: Redirect latency: p99 under 30 ms inside our data center for cached links, under 100 ms on a cache miss.
Redirect availability 99.99% (about 53 minutes of downtime a year); create availability 99.9%.
A created link is never lost: replicated synchronously before we return 201.
Click counts are eventually consistent: visible within 5 minutes, with at most 0.1% loss.
Generated codes are 7 characters and not guessable from each other.
outOfScope: Machine-learning phishing and malware detection (we will touch on abuse in follow-ups).
Rich analytics such as geography, device and unique visitors per link.
QR codes, link-in-bio pages, teams and billing.

assumptions: Each link is opened 80 times on average over its life (read:write = 80:1)
Peak traffic is 5× the daily average
About 500 bytes per link row including URL (avg ~200 chars), metadata and index overhead
About 10% of all links are opened on any given day

steps.label: Storage over 5 years
steps.math: 120 M × 60 months = 7.2 B links; 7.2 B × 500 B = 3.6 × 10¹² B
steps.result: ≈ 3.6 TB total, ≈ 720 GB after year one

steps.label: Code length
steps.result: 7 base62 characters keep the space 99.8% empty, so random codes rarely collide

steps.label: Redirect cache size
steps.math: 3 700/s × 86 400 s ≈ 320 M redirects/day; 10% of links active ≈ 32 M links/day × 500 B
steps.result: ≈ 16 GB: fits in one Redis node; use a small cluster for failover

steps.label: Click event volume
steps.math: 320 M clicks/day × 100 B ≈ 32 GB/day raw; aggregated to (code, day) rows: ≤ 32 M rows × 40 B
steps.result: ≈ 32 GB/day of events, ≈ 1.3 GB/day of daily counters

steps.label: Redirect bandwidth
steps.result: ≈ 9 MB/s at peak: not a concern

estimates.takeaway:
Creates are tiny: 230 writes/s at peak is nothing for one Postgres primary. The redirect path is 80× busier and the latency-sensitive part, so it gets a cache and stateless servers. The surprise is click counting: 3 700 counter updates per second is 80× the create rate, so it must not be an UPDATE on the link row. It goes through a queue and gets aggregated.

Storage reaches 3.6 TB over five years. That fits one large node for the first two to three years. After that we split the table by hash(code), and because every read is a lookup by code, that split is painless.

api.returns: 201 { code, shortUrl, expiresAt } · 409 alias taken · 422 invalid URL
api.note: The idempotency key is stored with the owner for 24 h, so a client retry after a timeout gets the same code back.
302 with Cache-Control: private, max-age=60, not 301, so expiry, edits and click counts keep working.
Owner only. Reads pre-aggregated daily rows, up to 5 minutes behind.
Owner only. Also deletes the cache entry so the change applies within seconds.
Soft delete: the code is never reused, so old printed links can never point to someone else's page.

entities.name: Link
entities.store: Postgres, one primary + 2 replicas; later split by hash(code)
fields: partial index where not null, for the sweeper
entities.why: One row per link. The hot query is a primary-key lookup by code. Aliases live in the same table, so the primary key alone enforces uniqueness across both.

entities.name: ClickEvent
entities.store: Kafka topic clicks, 32 partitions keyed by code, 7-day retention
fields: from the IP, IP not stored
entities.why: A buffer between the redirect path and counting. Redirect servers fire and forget, and the topic can be replayed if the aggregator has a bug.

entities.name: ClickDaily
entities.store: Postgres table (move to a columnar store if analytics grow)
entities.why: Stats pages read at most a few hundred rows per link. Storing daily totals instead of raw clicks cuts storage by about 25×.

data.note: Every redirect is SELECT url, expiresAt, deletedAt FROM link WHERE code = $1. A key-value store would also work, but Postgres gives us a unique constraint for aliases, transactions for idempotency keys and familiar operations. The partition key is code. Random codes spread evenly, so a later split into 8 shards by hash(code) needs no hot-shard handling. The only other index is (ownerId, createdAt) for the dashboard. It is low-traffic and can be served from a replica.

hld.summary:
Two stateless services sit behind one load balancer. The Link API handles creates, edits and stats. It is low traffic and talks to the Postgres primary. The Redirect service is the hot path. It checks a small in-process cache, then Redis, then a Postgres read replica. It answers with a 302 and publishes a click event to Kafka without waiting for it.

A Click aggregator consumes the topic, sums clicks per (code, day) in memory for about 30 seconds, and upserts the totals. A nightly Expiry sweeper marks expired links and cleans the cache. Servers keep no session state, so we scale either service by adding instances.

diagram.title: Create, redirect and click counting paths
diagram.src:

flows.title: Creating a link
steps: Link API validates the URL (scheme http/https, length ≤ 2 KB, not on the blocklist) and checks the owner's quota.
If an Idempotency-Key was sent and already stored for this owner, return the stored response.
With an alias: INSERT with code = alias. A unique violation returns 409.
Without an alias: generate 7 random base62 chars and INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. On conflict, retry with a new code (expected retries ≈ 0.002 per create).
Commit, with synchronous replication to one replica, then return 201 with the short URL.

flows.title: Opening a short link
steps: Redirect service looks up the code in its in-process LRU (5 s TTL, absorbs viral links), then in Redis.
On a miss, read the row from a replica and write it to Redis with TTL = min(1 h, time until expiry). Unknown codes are cached as 'missing' for 60 s.
If deleted or past expiresAt, return 410. Otherwise return 302 with the Location header.
Publish { code, ts, referrer, country } to Kafka asynchronously. If Kafka is slow, drop the event, never delay the redirect.

flows.title: Counting clicks
steps: The aggregator reads a batch from its Kafka partitions and adds to an in-memory map of (code, day) → count.
Every 30 s it upserts the map into ClickDaily (clicks = clicks + n) and records the Kafka offsets in the same transaction.
After a crash it resumes from the stored offsets, so no batch is counted twice.
The stats endpoint sums ClickDaily rows for the requested range.

deepDives.title: Generating short codes
deepDives.problem: We need 7.2 B unique codes over five years, created on many servers at once, without a single counter becoming a bottleneck or a single point of failure, and without codes that reveal their neighbours.

options.name: Hash the URL and take 7 characters
options.how: Compute SHA-256 of the URL (plus owner id), base62-encode it and keep the first 7 characters. On a collision with a different URL, add a salt and rehash.
pros: Same URL from the same owner always maps to the same code, so dedupe comes for free
No coordination between servers
cons: Collisions still need a check-and-retry path, so it is not simpler than random
Dedupe is often unwanted: two campaigns for the same URL need separate counts
Truncating the hash gives no better spread than random

options.name: Global counter, handed out in ranges, then scrambled
options.how: A counters table hands each server a block of 10 000 numbers. The server converts each number to base62 after passing it through a fixed reversible permutation, for example a small Feistel network over the 62⁷ space, so consecutive numbers give unrelated codes.
pros: Zero collisions, no retries
Uses the space densely, so 6 characters would last much longer
Block allocation means one counter write per 10 000 links
cons: More moving parts: block allocation, a permutation to get right and keep secret
A crashed server wastes the rest of its block (harmless, but codes are not contiguous)
If the permutation key leaks, codes become predictable again

options.name: Random 7 characters with a conditional insert
options.how: Draw 7 characters from a cryptographic random source and INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. If no row was inserted, draw again.
pros: Stateless and trivially correct: the database primary key is the only arbiter
Unguessable without any extra machinery
Works the same after we split the table, because the insert goes to the shard that owns the code
cons: The collision rate grows as the space fills: 0.2% per insert after 5 years at our volume
Every create is an insert that may fail, so it needs a retry loop
Cannot shorten to 6 characters later without collisions climbing to about 13%

deepDives.choice:
Random 7 characters with a conditional insert. At our numbers the space is 0.2% full after five years, so the expected number of retries per create is about 0.002. Write traffic is only 230/s, so an occasional retry costs nothing. It needs no counter service and gives unguessable codes for free.

What would change my mind: a requirement for 6-character codes, or volume high enough to fill more than about 10% of the space. Then the collision retries add up, and ranged counters with a scramble become worth their complexity.

deepDives.title: The redirect: 301 or 302, and where to cache
deepDives.problem: The redirect is 80× busier than creation and is what users feel. We want it fast and cheap, but links can expire, be deleted or be repointed, and owners want click counts. Caching too aggressively breaks both.

options.name: 301 Moved Permanently
options.how: Return 301. Browsers and proxies cache the redirect, often indefinitely, and later opens never reach us.
pros: Fewest requests to our servers
Fastest for repeat visitors
cons: We stop seeing repeat clicks, so counts are wrong
Deleting or repointing a link does not reach browsers that cached it, which matters a lot for a phishing takedown
No way to undo once sent

options.name: 302 with server-side caching
options.how: Return 302 with a short private max-age. Cache link rows in a per-process LRU (5 s) and in Redis (≤ 1 h), and fall back to a read replica.
pros: Every click reaches us and is counted
Deletes and edits apply within seconds when the API also deletes the cache key
Redis at 16 GB holds a whole day's active links
cons: Every redirect costs us a request, about 18 500/s at peak
Users far from our region pay the round trip

options.name: 302 cached at a CDN edge for a short time
options.how: Put a CDN in front with a 60 s edge TTL per code. Count clicks from CDN logs instead of from our servers.
pros: Low latency worldwide
Absorbs viral spikes before they reach us
cons: Counts arrive from log delivery, often minutes late
A takedown takes up to the TTL plus a purge call
Extra cost and another pipeline to run

deepDives.choice:
302 with server-side caching. Our 18 500/s peak is easy for a handful of stateless servers and one Redis cluster, and we keep exact control over deletes and counts. The in-process LRU with a 5 s TTL is there for one viral link at 50 000/s, so it does not hammer a single Redis shard.

What would change my mind: a global audience with a p99 target under 50 ms end to end, or traffic beyond 10×. Then I add the CDN layer and switch counting to edge logs.

deepDives.title: Counting clicks without slowing redirects
deepDives.problem: 3 700 clicks/s on average, with a viral link possibly taking 10 000/s alone. Updating a counter on the link row means row-lock contention on hot rows, WAL traffic on the primary, and a redirect that waits on a write.

options.name: UPDATE link SET clicks = clicks + 1
options.how: Increment a column on the link row inside the redirect request.
pros: Exact and immediately visible
No extra infrastructure
cons: Puts a primary write on the hottest path
A viral link serializes on one row lock
Redirect latency now depends on primary health

options.name: Redis INCR, flushed periodically
options.how: INCR clicks:{code}:{day} in Redis on each redirect, and a job flushes the counters to Postgres every minute.
pros: Sub-millisecond, simple
Redis handles hundreds of thousands of INCRs per second per shard
cons: A Redis failover loses up to a minute of counts
No raw events to replay if the logic changes
The flush job must be idempotent or it double counts

options.name: Event stream plus aggregator
options.how: Publish each click to Kafka without waiting. A consumer sums counts in memory and upserts (code, day) totals every 30 s, storing Kafka offsets in the same transaction.
pros: Redirect never waits on counting
Replayable for 7 days: fix a bug and recount
The same stream can feed abuse detection and richer analytics later
cons: Kafka is a new system to run if we do not have one
Counts are up to a minute or so late
Events are lost if the redirect server dies before sending its buffer

deepDives.choice:
Event stream plus aggregator, because the 5-minute freshness and 0.1% loss budget allow it, and replayability matters once counts turn into billing or a customer dispute.

What would change my mind: a small team with no Kafka. Then Redis INCR with an idempotent flush is fine at this scale. I would accept the risk of losing a minute of counts during a failover.

deepDives.title: Expiry, deletes and custom aliases
deepDives.problem: Expired links must stop working on time even when cached. Aliases and random codes share one namespace. Two users may race for the same alias, and a freed code must never start pointing somewhere new.

options.name: Delete expired rows and reuse codes
options.how: A job hard-deletes expired links and their codes return to the pool.
pros: Storage stays flat
Keeps the code space emptier
cons: A code printed on an old poster can start sending people to a stranger's page, which is a security problem
The space is 0.2% used anyway, so reuse buys nothing

options.name: Check on read, sweep lazily, never reuse
options.how: The redirect service compares expiresAt with the current time on every hit. The cache TTL is capped at the time left until expiry. A nightly sweeper sets deletedAt and evicts cache keys. Codes are never handed out again.
pros: Expiry is exact to the second, independent of the sweeper
No security issue from reuse
The sweeper can be slow or fail without users noticing
cons: Dead rows keep using storage (at most 3.6 TB, fine)
Every redirect does a timestamp check (trivial)

deepDives.choice:
Check on read, never reuse. For aliases, the same primary-key insert settles races. Whoever commits first wins and the other gets 409. We also keep a reserved-word list (api, admin, login…) and reject aliases that look like generated codes, so a random draw is less likely to hit a vanity name. When a user edits or deletes a link, the API deletes the cache key after the commit. The 60 s private browser max-age bounds how long any browser can still follow the old target.

What would change my mind: a legal need to erase data. Then expired rows are hard-deleted after a retention period, and the code moves to a tombstone table so it still cannot be reused.

failures: The Redis cluster restarts empty and redirects fall through to the database at up to 18 500/s
Read replicas sized for the full miss rate, request coalescing per code inside each redirect server, the in-process LRU, and pre-warming the top 1 M codes from yesterday's ClickDaily.
Automatic failover to the synchronous replica in about 30 s. Creates return 503 with Retry-After meanwhile. Redirects keep working from cache and replicas.
Redirect servers buffer up to 100 000 events in memory, then drop and increment a dropped-events metric. Redirects are never blocked. Alert if drops exceed the 0.1% budget.
One link goes viral at 50 000 opens/s

The in-process LRU (5 s TTL) serves it from every redirect server, so Redis sees about one read per server every 5 s. Kafka partitions by code, so one partition is hot. The aggregator pre-sums per batch, so this is fine.
Offsets are committed in the same Postgres transaction as the counter upsert, so on restart it reprocesses only the uncommitted batch and never double counts.
Someone enumerates codes to find private links
Random 7-char codes make blind guessing hit about 1 in 500 at the 5-year mark. Rate-limit 404s per IP, alert on 404 spikes, and let owners mark a link as requiring sign-in.
scale: 10× (460 creates/s, 185 000 redirects/s): split Link into 8 shards by hash(code) using consistent hashing, grow Redis to a 6-shard cluster, add redirect servers. Nothing changes in design.

100× (36 TB per 5 years, 1.85 M redirects/s): move links to a wide-column or managed key-value store keyed by code, run redirect servers and a read copy in every region, put a CDN in front with a 60 s TTL and count from edge logs.

Multi-region writes: give each region its own code prefix character, or keep random codes and a single writer region. With random codes, cross-region collisions are as rare as local ones, but the insert must go to the owning shard.

followups.q: How do you stop people from shortening phishing and malware links?
answer: Check URLs on create against a blocklist and a safe-browsing style reputation feed; reject or hold for review.
Re-scan links in the background, because a clean page can turn bad later. A takedown sets deletedAt and evicts the cache, which is why we use 302 and not 301.
Per-account and per-IP create quotas through the rate limiter. New accounts get lower limits.
Show an interstitial warning page for links flagged as suspicious instead of redirecting.

followups.q: If the same user shortens the same URL twice, should they get the same code?
answer: Ask the product question first. Usually no: separate campaigns want separate counts.
If yes, add a unique index on (ownerId, urlHash) and return the existing row. That is cheap at 46 creates/s.
Never dedupe across users, because owners have different expiry and stats rights.

followups.q: Owners now want unique visitors per day, not just clicks. What changes?
answer: Exact unique counts need a set of visitor ids per (code, day), which is far too much memory for 32 M active links.
Use a HyperLogLog sketch per (code, day): about 12 KB each for roughly 1% error, and sketches merge to give weekly totals.
Identify visitors by a hash of IP prefix plus user agent, or a first-party cookie. State the privacy trade-off.

followups.q: Your read replica lags and a brand-new link returns 404 right after creation. Fix it.
answer: The create response can write the new row straight into Redis, so the first open finds it in cache.
On a replica miss for a code younger than a few seconds, or on any miss, fall back to the primary once before returning 404.
Do not cache the 'missing' result when the primary was not consulted.

followups.q: How would you let enterprise customers use their own domain, like go.acme.com/x?
answer: Make the key (domain, code) instead of code. Each domain gets its own namespace, so aliases do not clash across customers.
Route by the Host header. TLS needs a certificate per domain, issued automatically after the customer adds a DNS record.
Cache keys and Kafka events carry the domain too.

mistakes: Spending ten minutes on code generation while ignoring that click counting is the largest write load in the system.
Returning 301 because it is 'faster', which silently breaks counts, expiry and takedowns.
Using a single auto-increment id encoded in base62, which lets anyone enumerate every link.
Designing a sharded NoSQL cluster on day one for 46 writes/s and under 1 TB in year one.
Writing analytics synchronously on the redirect path, so a slow analytics store slows every redirect.

mid: Asked about expiry, custom aliases and click-count freshness before drawing anything
Computed creates/s and redirects/s and concluded the system is read-heavy (about 80:1)
Chose a code length from the size of the keyspace (62⁷ vs links stored)
Put a cache in front of the database for redirects and named its size
Defined the create and redirect endpoints with status codes, including 404 vs 410
senior: Compared at least two code generation schemes and named their collision behaviour
Explained 301 vs 302 in terms of counts, edits and takedowns
Moved click counting off the redirect path, with an idempotent aggregation
Handled hot links with an in-process cache or request coalescing, not just 'add Redis'
Showed how alias races are settled by a unique constraint, not a read-then-write check
staff: Raised abuse (phishing, enumeration) and tied it back to design choices like random codes and 302
Planned the move from one database to shards by hash(code) with a trigger point (about 2 TB)
Discussed multi-region redirects and what CDN caching does to counting
Stated the click-loss budget and how they would measure it
